Ambivalence

/am-BIV-uh-lens/ — stress on second syllable, like 'divided' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Ambivalence is the state of having two conflicting feelings or opinions about something at the same time, making it hard to decide.

Her ambivalence about the move showed: she packed her bags, then unpacked them twice.

Worked Example

He stared at the acceptance letter to his dream school, thrilled by the opportunity yet devastated at leaving his close friends, his face reflecting his complete ambivalence.

Ambivalence is more precise than 'uncertainty' or 'confusion' because it specifically captures having two opposite feelings at once—not just being unsure. The tension between conflicting emotions is exactly what ambivalence names.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

conflict: A conflict is any clash of opposing forces — armies, arguments, or feelings fighting inside a person. It names the collision itself and fits struggles of every kind. Ambivalence is narrower and more exact: two opposite feelings aimed at the very same thing, pulling a person in both directions at once.

indecision: Indecision is being unable to settle on a choice — it describes the standstill you end up in. Ambivalence names what causes that standstill: holding two opposing feelings about the same thing. Indecision ends the moment you finally choose, but ambivalence can keep churning even after the decision is made.

wavering: Wavering is visibly tipping back and forth between options — leaning toward one choice, then drifting to the other. It describes the outward motion of a changing mind. Ambivalence is the inner condition underneath: two opposite feelings held at the same time, which can churn away even when you never budge.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

conviction: a firm, settled belief or certainty

certainty: complete sureness with no lingering doubt

Where it sits · how badly deciding gets blocked — doubt → hesitation → ambivalence → paralysis

doubt vs. ambivalence: Doubt is weaker than ambivalence — doubt is simple uncertainty about one thing, while ambivalence means two full opposing feelings tugging in different directions at once.

hesitation vs. ambivalence: Hesitation is milder than ambivalence: hesitation is a brief pause before acting, but ambivalence is a deeper inner tug-of-war between conflicting feelings.

paralysis vs. ambivalence: Paralysis is stronger than ambivalence — ambivalence makes deciding hard, but paralysis means the conflict is so overwhelming that no decision or action can happen at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ambi-

Prefix — ambi-: both, on both sides (Latin)

Root — val

Root — val: to be strong (Latin (valere))

Suffix — -ence

Suffix — -ence: state or quality of (Latin (-entia))

Put it together

Put it together: ambi- ('both') + val ('be strong') + -ence ('state of') literally means 'the state of being strong in both directions' — two powerful, opposing feelings pulling at the same time, which is exactly what ambivalence is. The word was coined in 1910 by psychologist Eugen Bleuler from these Latin pieces.

Use the root in a new word: valiant

Use the root in a new word: valiant: The valiant firefighter showed great strength and courage — the same Latin root val-, 'to be strong,' that gives ambivalence its sense of two strong feelings pulling at once.

Word Choice

formal / psychological

Ambivalence is the precise term when someone is genuinely torn between two opposing feelings or opinions. Use it when the conflict is real and significant enough to affect behavior, like hesitation about a decision. For milder uncertainty, 'doubt' works better; for situations where someone simply doesn't care, use 'indifference' instead.
